title: Continuity and Change

cards.h: Is Indian foreign policy new or the same old thing?
cards.b:
The central question is easy to state: has India's foreign policy changed since 1947, or only its style? UPSC asks it almost every few years, often as "continuity and change" or in the form of "Nehru to Modi".

The best answers say: core goals remain (sovereignty, security, development, strategic autonomy), while methods and partners have changed (from idealism to pragmatism, from the Soviet Union to many partners, from caution to assertive security action).

Use the phases below to structure your answer, and give each phase one date and one example.
These dates are rough. Some historians argue the real breaks were 1962 (Nehru's idealism was damaged), 1991 (economy) and 1998 (nuclear status).

• Strategic autonomy: from non-alignment to 'multi-alignment', India wants freedom of decision.
  • Panchsheel and respect for sovereignty (1954 agreement with China).
  • Priority to the neighbourhood: from Nehru's "special relations" to the Gujral Doctrine and Neighbourhood First.
  • Development as a goal: a stable external environment for growth.
  • Nuclear restraint: no first use, credible minimum deterrence, support for disarmament in speeches.
  • Support for the UN and the Global South, and a demand for UN reform.
  • No overseas bases or alliances.

A short way to say it: India has been a status quo power in territory and a reformist power in institutions.

• From idealism to realism: power and national interest are openly stated.
  • From Soviet closeness to multi-alignment: the US, Japan, France, Gulf and Russia all matter.
  • From moral lecture to action: India now acts (surgical strike 2016, Balakot 2019, Operation Sindoor 2025) and sets conditions.
  • From closed to open economy, so trade, energy and technology shape diplomacy.
  • New tools: diaspora events, digital public goods, solar alliance, vaccine diplomacy.

• Neighbourhood First (2014), Act East (2014), Link West / Think West, SAGAR (2015) and MAHASAGAR (2025).
  • Summit and diaspora diplomacy: Howdy Modi (Houston 2019), Namaste Trump (Ahmedabad 2020), large community events abroad.
  • Development partnerships: lines of credit, Vaccine Maitri (2021), Operation Ganga (2022) and other evacuations.
  • Climate and public goods: the International Solar Alliance, CDRI, Mission LiFE.
  • Economic nationalism with openness: Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat, PLI schemes, along with new FTAs.
  • Security doctrine: surgical strikes (2016), Balakot (2019), Sindoor (2025): the claim that India will respond to terror on its own terms, with no distinction between terrorists and sponsors.

Nehruvian idealism

Non-alignment, anti-colonialism, Asian solidarity, peace through the UN.

Indira Doctrine

No outside power should intervene in South Asia (a Monroe-style principle), and India will act where needed (Bangladesh 1971, Sri Lanka 1987).

Gujral Doctrine (1996–97)

Generosity towards smaller neighbours without reciprocity.

Vajpayee

Nuclear status, outreach to Pakistan (Lahore 1999), strategic partnership with the US.

Manmohan Singh

Civil nuclear deal; 'strategic autonomy'; G20 and BRICS.

Modi

Neighbourhood First, Act East, multi-alignment, 'new normal' on terror.

• C. Raja Mohan, Modi's World (2015): India has moved from "Nehruvian idealism" to pragmatic realism.
  • Shivshankar Menon, Choices (2016): successive governments made hard choices on China, Pakistan and the nuclear question.
  • Sunil Khilnani and others, Nonalignment 2.0 (2012): India should keep its autonomy but adapt it to a new world.
  • Kanti Bajpai: identifies Nehruvian, neo-liberal and hyper-realist schools that compete in Indian strategic thinking.
  • Tanvi Madan, Fateful Triangle (2020): India has long hedged between the US and China.
  • S. Jaishankar, The India Way (2020): argues that India must be a more confident player in a multipolar world, guided by multi-alignment and national interest.

Defenders of continuity (such as Menon) say India has always adapted its means. Those who stress change point to Modi's style: personal summit diplomacy, the diaspora, more willingness to use force, and a language of civilisation ('Vishwa Bandhu', 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam').

A balanced view: the objectives are continuous, the method is more assertive, and the world around India has changed more than India's basic aims.

• China: from Wuhan and Mamallapuram's summitry to Galwan's confrontation, then cautious re-engagement (Kazan 2024, Tianjin 2025).
  • US: from the nuclear deal and Quad to the shock of the 50% tariff (2025) and the 2026 trade framework.
  • Russia: Ukraine war neutrality; oil; Putin's visit (December 2025).
  • Pakistan: Sindoor and the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance.
  • Global South: G20 2023, BRICS chair 2026.

Each case shows both continuity (autonomy) and change (assertiveness, hedging, trade diplomacy).

"Indian foreign policy has shown continuity amid change. Discuss." (typical)
"Trace the evolution of India's foreign policy from Nehru to Modi." (typical)
"Is 'multi-alignment' a continuation of non-alignment or a break?" (typical)

Structure: (1) thesis in one line; (2) phases with dates; (3) continuity list; (4) change list; (5) scholars (Raja Mohan, Menon, Jaishankar); (6) test cases; (7) conclusion: same ends, new means.
